h: Jantar Mantar denotified: a move to push protest further from power
dek: Drawing on former judges, constitutional experts and historians, The Wire's analysis asks how a place that was never notified could be removed from the list of protest sites.
body: On 12 October Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites. The next day Cockroach Janata Party leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde, with a few companions, climbed over the barricades, were arrested and sent to five days of judicial custody. In its place the police suggested Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground, which the article says lie on the edges of the city.

The article shows that these options exist only on paper. Booking Ramlila Maidan can cost up to two lakh rupees, and it is said to be full for the next two and a half months. A journalist's video of the CBD Ground shows heaps of garbage, a stench and tall grass. The writer also points out that Jantar Mantar, a protest site since 1993, was never formally notified in the first place.

Constitutional expert G. Mohan Gopal argues that protest means bearing witness in front of everyone, and its place has been pushed steadily away from power: from Parliament to the Boat Club, from the Boat Club to Jantar Mantar, and now outside the city. A democratic government should keep protest close to power, and 'public order' should mean democratic order. In his view the government is turning the meaning of law and order upside down.

Former Supreme Court judge Gopala Gowda calls the decision unconstitutional and undemocratic, asks who gave the police commissioner this power, and says plainly that deep anger lies behind the protest. The article also recalls 2017, when the Green Tribunal banned protests here and, within a year, the Supreme Court set the ban aside, calling peaceful protest a basic right.

The article concludes that even in the digital age the public square has not lost its importance. From Tahrir Square to the wrestlers' sit-in and the anti-CAA protests, it is the place that gives a movement its face, and that is why taking it away is an attempt to snuff out dissent.
nazar: Moving protest from Jantar Mantar to a garbage ground is not just a matter of arrangements. It is a message that power does not want to hear the people's voice at its door. What is interesting is that, instead of weakening the movement, this step is making the picture of young people crossing barricades with the tricolour even bigger. The courts will now have to remember what they themselves said in 2018.
sawal: How do you remove a place that was never notified?
ref: Boat Club
The ground near India Gate where big sit-ins were held before 1993. After that, protests were sent to Jantar Mantar.
Tahrir Square
A square in Cairo that became the centre of Egypt's 2011 revolution, where a sit-in went on for months.

h: The other side's case: blame the newspapers' maths more than the Commission
dek: Right-wing commentator R. Jagannathan believes the media tossed around the figure of 13 crore deleted names without context, and that wrongly deleted names are less than half a per cent.
body: R. Jagannathan, former editorial director of Swarajya magazine, writes from the opposite side of this movement. His argument is that the real failure in the SIR belongs less to the Election Commission than to journalists who cannot read numbers. The Commission's mistakes can be corrected, but in his view reporters' weak arithmetic does violence to the truth.

He says the figure of 13 crore deleted names was repeated so often that it settled into people's minds, the way a shopkeeper first quotes a high price. By his count, about 2.8 crore of these were dead, 6.3 crore likely permanent migrants, one crore duplicate names, and roughly three crore recorded as absent at the time of the survey. Given 45 crore internal migrants in the country and about one crore deaths every year, he calls this natural.

The writer accepts that some people were wrongly removed, but estimates the number at under fifty lakh, that is, about half a per cent of roughly one billion voters. Those who were harmed speak up while 99 per cent stay silent, which he calls the psychology of 'loss aversion'. He also describes the criticism by former judges as exaggerated.

His conclusion is that the Commission did not conspire to keep voters out. Its real lapse was that in a country this large, where every figure runs into crores, it did not test its process beforehand. For the future he advises continuous cleaning of the rolls and a strong remedy for those wrongly removed.
nazar: We have placed this article here because the movement should know its opponents' strongest argument. But its figures are the writer's own estimates; the Commission has not made public the reason for each deleted name. And even half a per cent is fifty lakh human beings, most of whom are said to be migrants, poor people and minorities.

The article leaves out the biggest question: if it was only a mistake, why were names cut without notice, and why is the way back so narrow? A debate about counting cannot take the place of a debate about justice.
sawal: Is cutting fifty lakh names a small slip or a great injustice?
ref: Anchoring effect
The idea in psychology that the first figure you hear pulls every later estimate towards itself.

h: From the language movement to the Cockroaches: when the street bent the government
dek: This Al Jazeera explainer places the current uprising against the Election Commission in the line of big movements from 1965 to today, and looks at what the street won and what it did not.
body: In Delhi, surrounded by thousands of armed personnel, young people are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Yashraj Sharma's article places this uprising in India's old tradition in which the street has again and again forced governments to answer, though it has not always made them bend.

It begins in 1965, when an agitation flared up in Tamil areas against making Hindi the sole official language, and Prime Minister Shastri had to promise that English would continue; two years later the DMK won the state. Then came the JP movement, which led to the Emergency and, in 1977, to the first non-Congress government. In 1990, despite violent protests over the Mandal Commission's recommendations, the 27 per cent reservation for backward classes was finally upheld by the Supreme Court.

The article also shows that the street does not always win. Trade unions' protests against the 1991 economic reforms could not stop them. The Anna movement produced the Lokpal law, but its impact was slight. The Shaheen Bagh sit-in lasted 101 days, yet the citizenship law came into force in 2024. By contrast, farmers held out on Delhi's borders for a whole year, lost more than 700 of their own, and got all three laws withdrawn.

The Cockroach Janata Party comes next in this line. It was born out of a jibe at unemployed young people, and in July, protesting the NEET irregularities, it cost Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan his chair. According to the article, the current movement against the Election Commission is the next link in that chain and the toughest challenge yet for the Modi government, while the government keeps calling the protesters anti-national.
nazar: This history teaches one lesson: movements that keep their demand clear and concrete, as the farmers did with the repeal of three laws, are the ones that last and win. The movement against the Election Commission faces the same test: how firmly it holds, beyond the resignation, to a concrete demand such as restoring the voter list.
sawal: By what measure will the street's victory be judged this time?
ref: JP movement
A student movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan in 1974-75 that rose from Gujarat and Bihar, after which the Emergency was imposed.
Mandal Commission
A commission on backward classes, on whose recommendation 27 per cent reservation in central government jobs was brought in in 1990.

h: S.Y. Quraishi: trust is the Commission's real capital, do not squander it like this
dek: The former Chief Election Commissioner asks why a voter list that had become almost complete after seventy-five years of steady correction was suddenly put in the dock of suspicion in the name of the SIR.
body: Former Chief Election Commissioner S.Y. Quraishi believes a clean voter list is the foundation of democracy: dead, duplicate and ineligible names should be removed, but it is just as important that every eligible citizen's name stays. In his view the Commission did this work steadily for the past seventy-five years, and registration reached almost 99 per cent. So why suddenly abandon a working system for a Special Intensive Revision, the SIR?

Migration, urbanisation and duplicate names are old problems, and machinery for them already exists. He cannot understand why lists used in recent elections should now be treated as unreliable. In his reckoning, mere suspicion cannot be grounds for excluding anyone; every doubtful name needs its own inquiry, notice and hearing.

Citing Telangana, he says reports show that Form 7s filed in bulk were used to try to get genuine voters, mostly Muslims, removed, and on checking, all 30 voters in one case turned out to be genuine. In the SIR the relationship has been turned upside down: people who have voted for ten or twenty years are being asked to prove their link to old lists. More than 13 crore names were cut from the drafts across different phases, which cannot be brushed aside as a clerical slip.

Quraishi welcomes the Commission's step of matching old and new lists to add back those left out, but asks why the old list was not taken as the base from the start. If commissioners recorded objections, that is not an internal office quarrel. The agenda, the proceedings and the dissent should be made public.

His conclusion is that the Commission, created under Article 324, is not a government department. Public trust has been its greatest earning. The measure of integrity is not how many names were cut, but how accurate the list is.
nazar: This is not the voice of an agitator but of a man who has sat in that very chair, and that is why it carries weight. Quraishi does not even name Gyanesh Kumar, yet every question goes straight to Nirvachan Sadan (the Commission's headquarters): who took the decision, where is the dissent recorded, why is the burden on the citizen. This article is the technical basis for the demand of the young people seeking a resignation at Jantar Mantar.
sawal: Once trust is broken, how will the Commission earn it back?
ref: Article 324
The provision of the Constitution that gives the autonomous Election Commission full power to conduct elections, prepare the rolls and supervise them.
Form 7
The form used to object to a name on the voter list and have it removed. Giving false information is an offence under Section 31 of the 1950 law.

h: Rajkumar Agarwal: the court gave orders, the police ignored them; who is responsible?
dek: The editor of Atal Hind asks why the Supreme Court's orders did not reach the ground in Delhi on 10 and 11 October, amid thousands of detentions, closed metro stations and the rounding up of journalists.
body: Atal Hind editor Rajkumar Agarwal sees Delhi on 10 and 11 October as a test of all three: democracy, the police and the courts. Of the young people who gathered at the CJP's call to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, more than two thousand were detained, according to Reuters. The writer says stopping peaceful protest in the name of order is not justified.

RJD MP Manoj Jha's petition in the Supreme Court alleges more than six thousand detentions, cancelled trains and closed metro stations. The petition also alleges police misconduct with women protesters and three women journalists, and that the police stood by as spectators while people linked to the Bajrang Dal attacked. The writer wants these investigated and wants officers who shielded the attackers to answer for it.

On 11 October a bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said no one could be detained without legal process, the metro and trains should run, and journalists should not be stopped. Even so, according to reports, people including journalists were picked up near Connaught Place and the Press Club. The writer asks who is responsible for this gap between the order and the police's conduct.

He recalls Pakistan in 2007, when General Musharraf tried to remove Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry, lawyers and citizens came out on the streets, and the court restored him. At the same time he warns that Pakistan's judiciary is no model. Here, delays in bail and detention cases show that liberty is not always protected in time.

His demand is that the government and Delhi Police make public verified figures for detentions, arrests and FIRs, and that there be an independent inquiry into sexual misconduct and the detention of journalists. Questioning the court is not contempt; it is the hope that the court stays free of pressure from both the government and the mob.
nazar: The article's strength lies in its care: it calls every allegation an allegation, yet does not miss the real point. If a court's order does not reach the police station, it is a scrap of paper. A contempt notice has been issued; now we must see whether any officer is held accountable, or whether this too gets buried in a file like other notices.
sawal: Who will pay the price for ignoring the court's order?
ref: Contempt notice
On 11 October the Supreme Court issued a notice over the restrictions on the Delhi Metro and the alleged violation of its directions. A notice is not a finding of guilt.
The Iftikhar Chaudhry affair
The 2007 lawyers' movement in Pakistan against the attempt to remove the Chief Justice, after which he was restored.

h: Vishnu Nagar's satire: those who feel no shame become 'Gyanesh'
dek: Vishnu Nagar places the Chief Election Commissioner in a list of shameless powerful men from Netanyahu to Bush, one whose hands carry no blood, only names cut from the voter list.
body: Vishnu Nagar begins his satire by introducing a breed that feels no shame even after committing the worst crimes against humanity, because it believes it is protecting religion or the nation. Such people do not repent; in his telling, they simply become 'Gyanesh'. There is a long list: murder, gang rape, forgery, hate violence, fake encounters and Himalayas of lies.

The first example is Netanyahu, whom the writer holds responsible for the deaths of seventy thousand Palestinians. He calls the delegates who walked out at the United Nations moral cowards, and is still full of confidence. Nagar jokes that even after leaving office he will live comfortably and perhaps dream of making Israel a vishwaguru (teacher to the world) by 2047, a direct dig at our own slogan.

Then come Hitler and Mussolini, who met bad ends, but the writer says most killers die in bed under doctors' care. Despite the Iraq war, George Bush is living peacefully at eighty and may outlive his father.

India's Election Commission joins this line. After the Indian Express revelation, Nagar sketches a scene in which the Chief Election Commissioner clinks glasses with his two masters and laughs that there will be neither resignation nor jail. According to the writer, once the purpose is declared to be the defence of Hindutva, everything starts to seem justified.

The sharpest line in the satire is the difference between two forms of violence: the street thugs in saffron scarves, and the men in suits and glasses who cut names from the voter list. The writer says the second kind kill without killing, and not a single drop of blood shows on their hands.
nazar: Satire works by exaggeration, and many of Nagar's charges are his own political reading, not news. Still, the metaphor of violence in suits and glasses catches the pulse of today's movement: a person whose name was cut is a citizen, yet has fallen outside the count. 'Dead' voters arriving alive at Jantar Mantar is the answer to this very metaphor.
sawal: Is cutting a name also a form of violence?
ref: The Indian Express investigation
A September 2026 report giving details of written objections by two election commissioners to the SIR. The Commission called the disagreement normal.
Vishnu Nagar
Hindi poet, satirist and journalist, associated with the Janvadi Lekhak Sangh, who writes regular satire in Navjivan.

h: Rajendra Sharma's satire: Bharat Ratna or Padma Bhushan for Gyanesh babu?
dek: Writing in reverse, the editor of Lok Lahar asks why an officer who did such 'service' to democracy is getting demands for his resignation instead of a reward.
body: This satire by senior journalist Rajendra Sharma, editor of the weekly Lok Lahar, is written in ulti bani (saying things in reverse). In it, the opposition's demand for resignation is called ingratitude, and the real debate is over which honour Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar should receive for his service to democracy.

According to the satire, Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma wants to give him the Bharat Ratna, while Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya thinks the Padma Bhushan is enough. The writer quickly adds that even this disagreement is probably a rumour spread by opponents to cast doubt on the ruling side's unity.

Sharma's jibe is that Gyanesh Kumar, and Rajiv Kumar before him, 'saved' democracy, meaning they handled the voter list, the polling figures and the counting in such a way that power stayed where it was. According to the writer, those who call this vote theft simply do not grasp the depth of this 'service'.

He goes further: the easiest way to silence critics demanding resignation, it is suggested, is to remove the names of the voters who ask questions from the list too. No voter, no question. It also mocks a suggestion from some in the opposition that, instead of an award, he should simply be made prime minister.

In this way the whole piece becomes a charge sheet in the tone of praise. Every proposed honour is really an accusation, and every defence an admission that the Commission is no longer a neutral umpire; that is the writer's charge.
nazar: Ulti bani is an old and effective tradition of Hindi satire, and Sharma handles it with a steady hand. The suggestion to cut the names of those who ask questions makes you laugh less and fear more, because among crores of deleted names it has started to seem less of an exaggeration. If leaders of the ruling side really have come out in praise, the distance between satire and news shrinks further.
sawal: When praise itself sounds like an accusation, where does the umpire stand?
ref: Rajiv Kumar
The Chief Election Commissioner before Gyanesh Kumar, during whose term the 2024 Lok Sabha election was held.
Ulti bani
A way of speaking that comes down from Kabir, in which things are said in reverse so that the truth stings more.

h: Mahir Ali: fake ceasefires and a world sliding towards disaster
dek: In Dawn, Mahir Ali argues that Trump's 'energy ceasefire' is not for Ukraine but for the US midterm elections, and that Europe's rapid arming is raising the danger of a bigger war.
body: Mahir Ali begins with Donald Trump's 'energy ceasefire', announced on Sunday. Kyiv was surprised by it and Moscow silent. Zelensky said Ukraine would agree if Russia did, but the very next day he said six of Ukraine's energy sites had been attacked since the announcement.

According to the writer, the root of this deal is the price of diesel in America, which has almost doubled in Trump's second term. Most experts blame the US and Israeli war on Iran for this. Under the diesel arrangement with Moscow, recent sanctions on Russian business have been put on hold. Ali says the aim is to save the Republican Party in the November midterms, because if it loses both houses Trump fears a third impeachment. Anger over rising prices has reached Trump's own supporters.

He reminds readers that Trump has kept criticising Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil sites and has again talked of removing Zelensky and bringing in some obedient leader, while he has never said anything like that about Putin. The writer also believes a Democratic win would not solve Ukraine's crisis either.

Ali's deepest worry is about Europe. In his view Britain, France, Poland and Finland are arming so fast to prepare for a direct clash with Russia that they may be bringing that very clash closer. He sees the biggest danger in Europe's 'centrist' leaders, who sometimes disagree with Trump but are warlike in their own thinking.

In conclusion he says elections anywhere rarely change much these days, and the future of democracy may rest on the ability to fight misinformation. From Palestine to Ukraine, the drift of the writer's words is that showpiece ceasefires will not stop the world moving towards disaster.
nazar: The most important point in this article is that wars are now being decided by oil and diesel prices, not by human lives. Truck drivers, farmers and daily earners in India also bear the blow of tension in Hormuz and costly diesel. Instead of looking for its own gain in the bargaining between Russia and America, India should speak up for a real ceasefire.
sawal: Will a peace decided by the price of oil last?
ref: Energy ceasefire
Trump's proposal that Russia and Ukraine stop attacking each other's power and oil sites. It does not stop the war as a whole.
Midterm elections
Congressional elections held in America in the middle of a president's term, this time in November 2026.

h: Zahid Hussain: emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Pakistan's 'perfect storm'
dek: In Dawn, Zahid Hussain warns that dismissing a provincial government with a two-thirds majority and imposing governor's rule is moving Pakistan from 'hybrid' to 'hard' rule.
body: Journalist and author Zahid Hussain says that when emergency and governor's rule were imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, ruling leaders heaped praise on the move. He is reminded of the 1971 remark, 'Thank God, Pakistan has been saved', made after the military action in East Pakistan. He accepts the comparison is not exact, but says such action against a government with a two-thirds majority could make the atmosphere explosive.

Tension rose when the PTI threatened a march on Islamabad. The capital was sealed with containers and highways were closed. Talks between the government and the opposition broke down. According to the writer, the PTI's main demand, a meeting with Imran Khan and compliance with court orders, was never accepted. The emergency was imposed before Maulana Fazlur Rehman's mediation was complete, so to the writer the talks look like a cover for repression.

Now the provincial government is dissolved, Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and several ministers are in custody, and they face cases linked to the 9 May attacks and the threat of disqualification. An eleven-member advisory council, mostly technocrats, will work under the supervision of Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, but the real power lies with the establishment. Peshawar is under blockade, schools and colleges are shut, and internet has not been restored in many places.

Hussain's most serious warning is that isolated PTI workers could join hands with the TTP in troubled districts. A region with rising terrorism and a hostile border cannot be run from Islamabad or Rawalpindi without popular support. Removing a party with support across the country will only make things more unstable.

His conclusion is that the talk of 'resetting the system' is not aimed at restoring democracy but at strengthening dictatorship. The 26th and 27th amendments have tied the judiciary's hands, and new legal curbs have been placed on expression. In the writer's words, Pakistan is moving from hybrid to 'hard' rule.
nazar: Removing an elected government next door through an emergency is a warning for all of South Asia: the argument for suspending democracy in the name of 'security' sells easily everywhere. In India, the experience of Article 356 and Jammu and Kashmir shows that rule imposed from above breeds alienation, not peace. If the voice of the Pakhtun people is crushed, it is extremism that will gain ground.
sawal: How will any government fight terror without popular support?
ref: Governor's rule
Under Pakistan's constitution, handing a province's administration in an emergency to a governor appointed by the centre. The elected government is suspended or dissolved.
TTP
Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, a militant group active in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the tribal areas.

h: Navi Pillay's Nobel and the convenient conscience of international law
dek: In The Daily Star, Nowshin Nawal asks what it means that on the very day the world gave Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize, America imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
body: Barrister and columnist Nowshin Nawal writes that on 9 October South African jurist Navi Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize for human rights and international law, and on the same day America imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), where she was once a judge. The writer calls this deep dishonesty: celebrating justice while punishing its institutions.

Born in Durban in 1941, Pillay, as a woman of Indian origin, entered a profession that was never built for her. In 1967 she started her own practice in Natal and fought the cases of anti-apartheid activists and political prisoners. The writer says apartheid ran through laws, courts and offices, meaning discrimination had all its papers in order, so being legal and being just are not the same thing.

At the International Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay was a judge in the 1998 Akayesu case, which for the first time held that rape committed with intent to destroy a community can be genocide. She later became UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and chaired the commission of inquiry on Gaza, whose finding that Israel had committed genocide Israel rejected. The writer notes that a commission of inquiry is not a court, but the question is whether inquiries will depend on the political identity of the accused.

Nawal accepts that the objections of countries not party to the Rome Statute can be debated in law, but putting economic sanctions on a court is something else entirely. Eight countries including Canada, Germany, France, Britain and Japan opposed the sanctions, but the real test will come when investigations reach their own friends.

In conclusion she says the weaknesses of international law are real, but the answer is to strengthen institutions, not weaken them. A system that prosecutes the weak and spares the powerful is, in the writer's view, merely a hierarchy with a law degree.
nazar: Pillay's story holds two lessons for India. First, law itself can become a tool of injustice, and this applies to our own harsh laws too. Second, India is not a member of the ICC, and its silence on Gaza hollows out its claim to lead the Global South. A country that wants an equal world order must also speak out against impunity for the powerful.
sawal: Is justice only for weak countries?
ref: International Criminal Court
A court in The Hague that tries individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. America, India and Israel are not members.
Akayesu case
The Rwanda Tribunal's 1998 judgment, which for the first time recognised sexual violence as part of genocide.

h: Why taxing the small savings of the poor is wrong
dek: In The Daily Star, economist Mohammad Main Uddin argues that taxing interest on microfinance savings in Bangladesh will bring the government a small sum but weaken the safety net of poor families.
body: Main Uddin, professor of banking and insurance at Dhaka University, begins with a paradox. Bangladesh has 62 banks, yet only 28.3 per cent of people over 15 have an account with any financial institution. Banks shy away from lending to the poor because they demand collateral, small loans cost more to handle, and monitoring villagers or workers without a fixed address is expensive.

The writer points out that the banks' own record is not good either: the bad loan rate is 32.78 per cent, which he calls the highest in the world. Microfinance institutions filled this gap, lending without collateral to groups of five to ten people. According to the writer, these institutions reach about 91 per cent of the poor, most of them women, and 95 per cent of loans are repaid.

Now the National Board of Revenue has moved to tax the interest on savings held in these institutions. The writer does the sums: by June 2026, 633 licensed institutions held 95,720 crore taka in savings; at an average interest of eight per cent that comes to about 7,658 crore taka, and a ten per cent tax would bring the government about 766 crore taka. A small sum for the government, a big one for poor savers.

His argument is that these savers are below taxable income anyway, so taxing their savings like bank deposits is unjust. Savings are a support in times of illness, floods, crop failure and lost jobs. If savings fall, dependence on loans and the grip of moneylenders will grow; one study found their interest rates going up to 250 per cent.

The writer's conclusion is simple: banks take deposits from the poor but do not lend to them, while microfinance invests the village's money in the village. The government should withdraw this decision.
nazar: This debate is just as true for India. Here, lakhs of women who rely on self-help groups and small savings schemes take the blow of changes in interest rates and taxes in every budget, while big corporate loans are written off. At the same time it is not right to romanticise microfinance either: reports of suicides under the pressure of loan recovery are also part of this story.
sawal: Why tax the poor man's savings and forgive the rich man's loans?
ref: Microfinance
Institutions that give small loans without collateral and savings facilities to the poor, especially groups of women. Bangladesh's Grameen Bank is the famous example.

h: Bharat Dogra: the right to information is weakening and must be saved
dek: In Countercurrents, Bharat Dogra cites a new review to show that years-long waits at information commissions have blunted the RTI law, a law born of the struggle of village workers.
body: Bharat Dogra, a journalist long associated with the RTI movement, recalls two old Supreme Court judgments that stressed citizens' right to know how the government works. He then says the working of the Right to Information law has become much weaker, mainly because appeals take so long to be heard.

According to the latest review by Satark Nagrik Sangathan, 12 of 25 information commissions, including the Central Information Commission, have waits of a year or more. Two commissions are not functioning at all, and in three states the wait stretches to 18-19 years. As of 30 June 2026, 3,85,716 appeals and complaints were pending. The Gujarat and Karnataka commissions have kept the wait to about a month, which shows that things can change where there is the will.

A large part of the article is about the law's history. The 2005 law was the result of nearly fifteen years of campaigning, and the demand came from Rajasthan's farmers and workers, whom the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan had brought together over jobs and drought relief. Public hearings by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh exposed irregularities in panchayat (village council) funds, and some representatives promised to return the money.

Dogra lists many such experiments: the exposure of a ration scam in Nokha, Bikaner; rigged panchayat records in Hardoi; and in Barwani, the Adivasi Mukti Sangathan showing that drought relief work went to contractors with machines and that wages were recorded in the names of people who were absent. In Delhi's settlements too, women's groups made it a tool for their right to rations.
His conclusion is that RTI has proved its strength both before and after it became law, and people's demand for it is still alive. What is needed is to fix the flaws in its working at once.
nazar: RTI's weakness is not just an administrative slip. Empty chairs in the commissions, the 2019 amendment that reduced the independence of information commissioners, and new exemptions linked to the data protection law are together blunting the tool the poor used to demand accounts of their rations, wages and pensions. In an age when the government wants to dodge every question, the fight for RTI is a fight for democracy.
sawal: What use is information that arrives eighteen years later?
ref: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan
An organisation started in 1990 at Devdungri in Rajasthan, whose public hearings gave rise to the right to information movement.
Information commission
Bodies set up at the centre and in the states, where one appeals when an RTI request gets no answer.

h: Sunita Narain: Delhi's air needs real work, not a shutdown of the city
dek: In Down To Earth, Sunita Narain argues that the government's new pollution plan shuts the city and puts the burden on people, when what is needed is time-bound work on public transport and clean fuel.
body: Sunita Narain writes that Delhi's winter pollution season is beginning, when toxic particles settle close to the ground and smoke from stubble burning in neighbouring fields makes it worse. The government has announced measures, which she sees as a sign of concern for public health, but also as inadequate and weak.

Her objection is that the plan shuts the city and shifts responsibility onto people. Private vehicles are a big source, but curbs on them will only work when people have buses, the metro and safe walking and cycling routes. The direction to run offices at half capacity from November to January is part of the same thinking.

Narain speaks from experience. As a member of the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority, she took the idea of the Graded Response Action Plan to the Supreme Court in 2016. In her view it was an emergency warning for smog, not a substitute for real work. In the original plan notified in 2017, schools could be closed only at the 'severe' or 'emergency' level. The drift of her words is that shutdown was never meant to be policy.

She recalls that the court had laid the groundwork by 2019: at least 10,000 buses for the city, an expanded metro and the Delhi-Meerut rapid rail. Today Delhi has about 6,840 buses, and there is almost no connection between the other cities of the NCR. Welcoming the electrification of buses, she says it is incomplete without a strategy to increase ridership. Factories in unauthorised areas have been told to give up coal, but no arrangement has been made for cheap electricity or gas.
Her conclusion is that the problem is that work is not happening at scale. Bringing the pollution graph down needs strict, time-bound steps.
nazar: The biggest price of shutting the city is paid by daily-wage workers, street vendors, construction workers and children who have no means to study at home. Putting the burden of clean air on those who pollute least is turning things on their head. And before blaming farmers for stubble burning, we should also ask where governments are in giving them alternatives.
sawal: Who, in the end, will pay the price of clean air?
ref: GRAP
An emergency plan, notified in 2017, to impose stage-by-stage restrictions in Delhi-NCR according to the level of air quality.
EPCA
An authority set up in 1998 at the Supreme Court's direction to monitor Delhi's pollution. In 2020 it was replaced by the Commission for Air Quality Management.

h: After three decades, Jantar Mantar loses its status as a protest site
dek: Delhi Police has removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and suggested two places outside the city and Ramlila Maidan. Activists call it a move to suppress dissent.
body: In New Delhi, the road by an eighteenth-century observatory, a short distance from Parliament, has been the country's best-known protest site since 1993. According to an AFP report carried in Dawn, Delhi Police issued an order on Monday saying Jantar Mantar is no longer a notified place for protests. The police cited a Supreme Court direction that asked for other suitable places to be fixed for protests.

Three places have been set aside as alternatives: two on the outskirts of the capital and Ramlila Maidan for large crowds. The decision came after a clash with an online youth movement called the Cockroach Janata Party, which has been gathering thousands of people over the revision of the voter list and the demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. On 13 October there were also protests in Patna and Ahmedabad.

On Wednesday two senior party leaders who crossed the barricades to 'take back' Jantar Mantar were sent to jail for five days on charges of alleged trespass. Founder Abhijeet Dipke says the place is not just an address but the spirit of resistance. Activist Shabnam Hashmi called it an attempt to rein in dissent and said protest here had already been squeezed by limits on space and time.

Activists argue that the site's strength was its nearness to Parliament, ministries and the media, and that moving it away will hurt the crowds, the attention, and the pockets of those coming from other states. Some local residents complained about noise and closed roads, and former police commissioner Kiran Bedi defended the decision. One protester said people would keep gathering there, and then the police took him away.
nazar: The road where farmers, wrestlers and the unemployed carried their message to the country has been closed at exactly the moment the biggest movement is standing there. It is hard to call that a coincidence. In a democracy the place of protest should be where power can hear it, not in some ground outside the city.
sawal: Should the place of protest be out of power's sight?
ref: Jantar Mantar
An eighteenth-century observatory in Delhi. Since 1993 the road beside it was the official protest site.
Cockroach Janata Party
An online youth movement that is out on the streets against the voter list revision and the Election Commission.
photo_note: Representative photo: Jantar Mantar, New Delhi

h: Thousands of applications to cut votes in Andhra, with no record of why
dek: A News Minute investigation: in more than half of the over 40 thousand applications to delete names filed in the last twelve days, the objector is the election officer himself, and no reason is recorded.
body: During the Special Intensive Revision of the voter list in Andhra Pradesh, the window for claims and objections ran from 31 July to 10 October. The News Minute went through the data from 29 September to 10 October, because older files stay online for only a week. In these twelve days objections were filed under Form 7 against 40,006 names, and in 20,959 of these cases, about 52 per cent, the objector is the Electoral Registration Officer or an assistant.

The problem is that when an ordinary citizen fills Form 7, the Commission's list shows the reason for deletion, such as death, change of address or a duplicate entry, but when an officer objects, the reason column stays empty. In the twenty constituencies with the most deletions, this share goes up to 77 per cent. In Narasapuram 94 per cent, in Palakol 90 per cent and in Chandragiri 81 per cent of cases list the officer as the objector.

Two officers and an assistant said that from their login in the ERO Net software they can only approve or reject, the reason is not shown, and the actual applications come with papers from family members or booth agents. One officer cited more than three thousand deaths in his area, some from spurious liquor.

Former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa says software should follow the rules, not rules the software. According to T.R. Meena, former Chief Electoral Officer of Kerala, this app has created a mess and no one knows how many names were rightly cut. Questions were sent to the state's Chief Electoral Officer Vivek Yadav, but no reply had come by the time of publication.
nazar: A voter whose name is cut has the right to know why. When half the applications have no reason recorded, the road to appeal also closes. This investigation shows that transparency is not only a question of intent but also of the machinery the Commission has built.
sawal: Whose job is it to record why a name was cut?
ref: Form 7
The form for objecting to a name on the voter list to have it removed. One of five fixed reasons has to be chosen.
ERO
Electoral Registration Officer, legally responsible for the voter list of a constituency.

h: Beaten in the detention van, held 40 kilometres away: a journalist's eyewitness account
dek: M Rajshekhar describes how protesters picked up from Connaught Place on 11 October were beaten in a police van and held in a community hall in Pandwala Khurd.
body: Around four in the afternoon on Sunday 11 October, students of the Disha Chhatra Sangathan were shouting slogans against the Chief Election Commissioner, the Prime Minister and the Home Minister on the Outer Circle of Connaught Place. Journalist M Rajshekhar was taking photographs when the police picked him up too. According to him, passers-by were picked up along with the protesters and held, surrounded, on the road near Regal Cinema.

The writer alleges that almost everyone who climbed into the blue van with mesh windows was beaten by three policemen. He himself was not hit, but he saw five of the six people in his cage-like section being beaten. Lawyer and activist Arjun Unnikrishnan also alleged beatings in the van. Phones had already been taken without a receipt, so that no video could be made.

The van went first to Chawla police station and then to a community hall in Pandwala Khurd, about 40 kilometres away. There one young man had a broken arm, one had a bleeding nose and a Sikh boy had chest pain. Medical help came late. The power was out and people sat in the light of vehicle headlights. At nine at night lawyers and people from the PUCL arrived; only then did the police soften, and the minors were released.

The writer says that last week 45 metro stations were shut and buses coming to Delhi were stopped. In his view this attempt at intimidation is backfiring, because people have begun to see protest as their democratic right. Questions were sent to Delhi Police, but no reply came.
nazar: This report is valuable because it is not rumour but the testimony of an experienced journalist, with times, places and names on record. The court has already said that journalists' work must not be obstructed. The question now is who will investigate the beatings in custody.
sawal: Who will fix accountability for beatings in custody?
ref: PUCL
People's Union for Civil Liberties, a civil rights organisation founded in 1976.
Pandwala Khurd
A village near Najafgarh in south-west Delhi, about 40 kilometres from Connaught Place.

h: UAPA against Siang dam protest, gatherings banned in Upper Siang
dek: In Arunachal, four people protesting an 11,000 megawatt project were detained under the state's UAPA law, and then gatherings of more than five people were banned.
body: In Arunachal Pradesh's Upper Siang district, the administration banned gatherings of five or more people on 11 October. According to Mongabay India, the order came amid growing protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, and two days earlier four protesters had been detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014.

This is an 11,000 megawatt hydropower project that will submerge 27 villages, including the district headquarters Yingkiong. People of Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang have been opposing it steadily. After Chief Minister Pema Khandu's visit, the protests turned violent in early October, with allegations of vehicles being burnt and of people entering an MLA's house, and there are allegations of a police lathi charge on 4 October.

On 13 October the Adi Bane Kebang United, the youth wing of the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum and the youth organisation of the affected area gave a memorandum to the district magistrate. The demands are: unconditional release of those detained, withdrawal of the central armed forces, a halt to the dam's feasibility study, and withdrawal of cases. District magistrate Ashok Tajo says the area is calm and the detentions can be challenged before the state government.

The UAPA and the bans have come after allegations that the movement gets foreign money. Bhanu Tatak, legal adviser to the farmers' forum, received a notice from a central agency alleging he took 17 lakh rupees without registration under the foreign contribution law. The protest is against NHPC's pre-feasibility study, one of the last studies before the detailed project report.
nazar: When Adivasi (indigenous) villages stand up to save their land and river and the answer is an anti-terror law, this is a story not of development but of a decision imposed without consent. The charge of foreign money is an old weapon used against every movement, and it is yet to be proved.
sawal: Can a dam be decided without the villages it will drown?
ref: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project
A proposed 11,000 megawatt hydropower project on the Siang river in Arunachal, to be built by NHPC.
Adi community
The main Adivasi community of the Siang valley, whose traditional council is called the Kebang.

h: Chromium a thousand times the limit in Nashik borewells, 109 people with skin disease
dek: Yellow water was coming out in the Dattanagar settlement of the Ambad industrial area. Tests found toxic hexavalent chromium, and 17 electroplating units were shut down.
body: About 25 thousand people live in the Dattanagar settlement of the Ambad industrial area in Nashik, Maharashtra. According to Down To Earth, people had been complaining for about a month that yellow water was coming from their borewells. Groundwater pollution is now being investigated within a radius of about 500 metres.

An independent test commissioned by SANDRP found hexavalent chromium at 50.3 milligrams per litre, while the Bureau of Indian Standards sets the limit for total chromium in drinking water at 0.05 milligrams, that is, more than a thousand times over. The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board's test on 8 October found 45 milligrams in two samples. The International Agency for Research on Cancer considers this chemical carcinogenic to humans.

The municipal corporation examined 248 people, of whom 109 had skin disease or allergies. SANDRP has spoken of rashes, blisters and deep wounds that are slow to heal, and swollen glands in some women and children. Two women are reported to have had miscarriages, though the report says clearly that this cannot yet be linked to chromium. According to one medical officer, the illnesses are mild.

The pollution board has shut 17 electroplating units, sealed eight borewells, and water is being supplied by tanker. On 17 October a camp will be held to take blood and urine samples. According to SANDRP, some workers' families are spending half their earnings on treatment, rented rooms and dressings.
nazar: The workers' settlements near industrial areas are the first to drink the poison, and units are shut only a month after the complaint. The real question is who has been dumping waste into the ground for years, and who will pay for the damage.
sawal: When will the polluting units bear the cost of treatment?
ref: Hexavalent chromium
A toxic form of chromium that comes from electroplating and the leather industry and causes cancer.
SANDRP
South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People, a group that works on rivers and water.

h: Pakistan orders TV channels not to broadcast blasts and attacks live
dek: Amid the emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PEMRA has said channels must show only information confirmed by a government department, or face legal action.
body: The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority, PEMRA, has told all satellite TV channels not to broadcast, rebroadcast or cover live any untoward incident such as an explosion, firing or terrorist attack. According to Dawn's Islamabad correspondent Kalbe Ali, the paper has seen this order dated 13 October.

Under the order, channels may show only information confirmed by the department concerned or a law enforcement agency. They must keep a delay mechanism in their broadcasts and set up an independent editorial board. PEMRA has cited its own laws, a 2018 suo motu judgment of the Supreme Court and a 2022 order of the Islamabad High Court, and recalled a similar direction from February 2023.
Violations carry a warning of action under Sections 29-A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance 2002. These sections open the way to anything from fines to suspension of licences.

The order comes at a time when the federal government on Sunday imposed governor's rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, saying the provincial government had deliberately kept away from counter-terrorism efforts. Before this, the PTI had announced a long march to Islamabad for Imran Khan's release. On Tuesday a PTI protest in Bara tehsil turned violent, government buildings were set on fire and there were clashes with the police.
nazar: The argument for reining in sensational coverage of attacks is understandable, but the rule of 'only government-confirmed information' turns news into a government statement in the middle of an emergency. When the people's elected government has been removed in an entire province, independent reporting from there matters most.
sawal: In an emergency, who will tell the truth, the channels or the government?
ref: PEMRA
Pakistan's electronic media regulator, which issues licences for TV and radio.
Governor's rule
Administration in the hands of a governor appointed by the centre, in place of the province's elected government.

h: Cheruvayal Raman: the keeper of seeds is gone
dek: In Down To Earth, K.A. Shaji remembers how Raman, a Kurichiya farmer of Wayanad, saved 64 native varieties of rice from the age of 17, and how to the very end his only worry was that the seeds should survive.
body: Cheruvayal Raman, a farmer of Kammana village near Mananthavady in Kerala's Wayanad, whom people fondly called Rametten, has died at 74 after a brief illness. His ancestral mud house was always full of sacks of seed, and every sack had its own name and its own story. He was 17 when, after his maternal uncle died, the responsibility for the traditional seeds entrusted to the family fell to him.

Raman belonged to the Kurichiya community, a Scheduled Tribe known in Malabar for growing rice. He kept 50 native varieties from Wayanad and 14 from other parts of Kerala: deep red-grained Chennellu, Veliyan for kanji (rice gruel), the fragrant Gandhakasala and Kayama, and Navara, used in medicine and rituals. He gave seeds away without taking money, especially to Adivasi (indigenous) families.

According to the writer, Wayanad once had around 160 native varieties. Coffee, pepper, ginger, areca nut and construction swallowed the fields, costs rose and rice became a losing proposition. In this situation Raman's fields were a living gene bank. He gave up chemical fertiliser in 1978 because the soil was losing its life, and he used to say that farming should feed the soil, not kill it.

He received many honours: the Padma Shri in 2023, the Centre's Genome Saviour Award, and a post as professor of practice at Kerala Agricultural University. But he bore the yearly cost of about 70,000 rupees to keep up the collection himself, storage depended on the coolness of the mud house, and at times the household ran on ration rice. He used to say that seeds cannot wait for speeches.

His biggest worry was that the land would pass to relatives and perhaps no rice would be sown there. Shaji writes that what is urgently needed now is money, secure land, proper storage and joint work by researchers and Adivasi communities, while respecting the communities' rights and knowledge.
nazar: Raman's story is a mirror of India's farm policy: it gave him the Padma Shri, but left the cost of saving seeds to the pocket of an Adivasi farmer. As the climate turns harsher, native varieties that can withstand drought and floods are the capital of food security, and this capital lies mostly in the homes of farmers like him.
The true tribute to him would be for his seeds to survive not locked in some government store but in the hands of the Kurichiya community, along with the community's rights.
sawal: How many varieties have been orphaned by the passing of one farmer?
ref: Kurichiya
An Adivasi community of Wayanad and Malabar, known for rice farming and for the 1812 revolt against the British.
Landraces
Local crop varieties chosen and saved by farmers over generations. They have qualities that help them withstand harsh weather.

h: Bandung 1955: when newly free nations frightened the great powers
dek: Al Jazeera's new short documentary tells the story of the conference where 29 countries of Asia and Africa claimed their place in the post-colonial world, and asks why its questions are still alive today.
body: On 28 September Al Jazeera English released a film of about twelve and a half minutes in its 'Al Jazeera Originals' series, titled 'Bandung: The Meeting That Scared the Superpowers'. It appeared on YouTube with the question of what happens when countries stand up to the great powers. The film's subject is the Asian-African Conference held in April 1955 in the Indonesian city of Bandung.

According to the film's page, 29 countries that had recently become free or were on the road to freedom gathered at that conference. They rejected colonial rule and declared their intention to break out of a system that, in the spirit of the film's words, had been built against them. The host was Indonesia's President Sukarno, and leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru from India, Zhou Enlai from China and Gamal Abdel Nasser from Egypt were present; this is well recorded in history.

The film claims this meeting did not remain a one-day event but became a movement. It influenced people from Nelson Mandela to Malcolm X, and gave the countries of the Global South a new sense of their own strength. The Non-Aligned Movement formed later in 1961, in which India played a big role, is seen as a link in the same chain.

The film also promises to show the other side of that era. According to it, the imperial powers answered this unity with coups, economic pressure and attempts to divide countries. During the Cold War years the elected governments of several newly independent countries were toppled; that is well-known history of the period. Even so, the film says, the idea of Bandung did not die.

The film rests on rare archival footage and the analysis of experts. It does not merely recall that era but asks why the questions about power and sovereignty raised at Bandung still matter today: who sets the rules of the world, and who pays their price.

That question becomes sharper in today's climate. Amid tariff wars over trade, the war in West Asia and the dominance of powerful countries in international institutions, small and poor countries are once again asking what was asked seventy years ago. The film is short, but it tries to link a forgotten chapter to today's debate.
nazar: Bandung is part of India's own story. In Nehru's time India saw itself not as the follower of any bloc but as a voice of the countries that had emerged from colonialism. Today, when our foreign policy seems to have shrunk to bargaining with powerful countries and our voice on questions like Palestine has grown faint, this film reminds us that India was once in the front row of those who spoke of equality.

The spirit of Bandung was not only about equality between nations but also about the dignity of people. The true heir to that legacy can only be a country that also gives equality to the marginalised within its own borders.
sawal: Can today's India raise the voice of Bandung?
ref: Bandung Conference
A meeting of 29 countries of Asia and Africa in Bandung, Indonesia, in April 1955. Ten principles on opposing colonialism and mutual cooperation were agreed here.
Non-Aligned Movement
A group of countries started in Belgrade in 1961 that did not join either the American or the Soviet bloc. Nehru, Nasser, Tito, Sukarno and Nkrumah were its leaders.

h: Naipaul's jasmine: the language his own, the literary tradition not
dek: On Jankipul, a Hindi translation of V.S. Naipaul's 1964 essay 'Jasmine', the story of a writer raised in a colony and his tangled relationship with English.
by: V.S. Naipaul (translated by Ashutosh Kumar Thakur)
body: Jankipul has published a Hindi translation of V.S. Naipaul's short 1964 essay 'Jasmine', done by the young writer Ashutosh Kumar Thakur. The moderator's note calls it an important document of colonial influence on English and of the attempt to break free of it. The essay turns on a difference: the daffodil he read about but never saw, and the jasmine he knew but whose name he did not know.

Naipaul begins with a memory from the days of a literary programme on the BBC's Caribbean service, when a writer from Trinidad came with his manuscripts. Then he goes back to his childhood. The English literature taught at school felt to him like some foreign mythology. Wordsworth's daffodils meant nothing to him, and he would carry Dickens's London to Trinidad in his mind, putting the rain of hot countries in place of the fog.

His argument is that literature needs social truth. The class-bound world of English novels was unknown to him, and his own life in Trinidad could not become literature until someone gave its streets and people words. A few unpublished Trinidadian stories showed him how art sorts and shapes raw experience, and how the familiar streets of one's own town gain dignity in literature.

The essay's central line is that English is his language, but its literary tradition is not his. Studying English literature at university in England felt dry and bookish to him; he found more joy in the language of Chaucer and Shakespeare. He also questions English fiction's obsession with social comment.
It ends in British Guiana, where, on asking about the scent of a flower, he is told it is called jasmine. But even then the word and the flower do not become one in his mind.
nazar: To a Hindi reader this essay will not feel strange. For years our school books too were full of flowers, seasons and heroes that were not around us, and the world of our own speech had to fight for a place in literature. There has been disagreement with much of what Naipaul said, especially his views on India and Islam, but he caught this rift between language and experience with great honesty.
sawal: Can a flower whose name you do not know enter a poem?
ref: V.S. Naipaul
Writer (1932-2018) born in Trinidad into a family of Indian origin. He received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2001.
Daffodil
The yellow flower of Wordsworth's famous poem, learnt by rote in colonial schools. It became a symbol of how foreign English literature felt.

h: Pinjra Tod: the question beyond the nine o'clock gate
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, a student writes about her first protest at Allahabad University, and on the way back gets stuck on the hostel curfew.
body: On the evening of six October, people began to gather in front of the women's hostel of Allahabad University. According to the writer, within a short time there were three to three hundred and fifty people there, many of them boys. This was a 'Pinjra Tod' (Break the Cage) protest, raising demands for women's freedom, equality and safety.

At the time Nandini was rehearsing a play at Swaraj Vidyapeeth right across the road. When the sound of slogans came inside, her focus broke. The teacher said to finish the scene first, but neither her mind came back nor those of her fellow actors. In the end the whole troupe was let go and they joined the crowd. The drums kept beating, the procession went from the hostel to Chandrashekhar Azad Park, speeches were made there, and according to the writer there was no vandalism or violence anywhere.

She writes that things one thinks about alone take on a different strength when spoken together with a crowd. She especially liked the boys taking part, because equality cannot be women's burden alone.

The real turn comes on the way back. On the road the girls were looking at the clock: it was already eight, and the hostel gate would close at nine. This is where the writer's question arises: why is it always a woman's freedom that gets cut in the name of safety, and why is a girl who stays out late seen as the problem, and not the lack of a safe environment?

In the end she accepts that one protest does not break patriarchy, but the small cages, such as time limits, fear and people's stares, start to become visible. It also bothered her that different organisations began raising their own separate slogans, when the shared purpose should have stayed at the centre.
nazar: Pinjra Tod's demands are ten years old, yet curfews on campuses are still only for girls. Nandini's piece is valuable because it is not the statement of a leader or analyst but of a student out on the street for the first time. When young people are on the streets across the country, it is worth remembering that the fight for freedom also begins at the hostel gate.
sawal: Why doesn't the hostel gate close at nine for boys?
ref: Pinjra Tod
A women students' campaign that began in Delhi in 2015, against discriminatory hostel rules and curfews.
Bela
Hindwi's daily blog section, with essays, memoirs and comment on literature, society and culture.

h: Five poems of Anne Carson in the hands of a psychiatrist poet
dek: On Jankipul, Patna psychiatrist and poet Vinay Kumar has rendered five poems by Anne Carson into Hindi, ranging from grief to tender attention.
body: Hindi translations of Canadian poet and classics scholar Anne Carson are appearing in large numbers these days. According to Jankipul's moderator, this offering stands apart because of its translator. Vinay Kumar is a counselling psychiatrist in Patna, known in his profession in India and abroad, and also the poet of collections such as 'Pani Jaisa Desh' (A Country Like Water) and 'Mall Mein Kabootar' (Pigeons in the Mall). The note says his poetry, like Carson's, crosses the borders between forms.

The first poem is about a daughter who wears her late father's old blue cardigan, in the very place where it used to hang. The father's habits, a chilly memory of a summer day and his strange, childlike restlessness all come through images of winter and night. The second poem, 'City of the Angel', is about the growing, hardening distance between those left behind after a death, made bitter by a long simile of an old woman's fallen teeth.

The third poem is a small, somewhat sad joy of love: night, closed eyes, and the beloved fixing things by the roadside with a small box of tools. At the end there is a plea for a new world, because the speaker is no longer the same as before.

'Brooklyn Room' is the calmest and most sensuous poem, in which a slow afternoon, a few sounds and light trembling on the ceiling wash away the time of the clock. The last and shortest poem is made of an old man's words on the return of spring, rain on closed windows and a distant longing.
All five poems are in free verse and move between grief, parting, tenderness and stillness. The poems cannot be reproduced here; they should be read on Jankipul itself.
nazar: A psychiatrist translating Carson is interesting in itself, because Carson's poetry looks at grief and the breaking of the mind without noise. In the rush of translations after the Nobel, it is worth remembering that translation is not just changing words but settling a sensibility into another language.
sawal: Is it possible to translate grief?
ref: Anne Carson
Canadian poet, essayist and scholar of Greek literature, born in 1950. 'Autobiography of Red' and 'Nox' are among her well-known books.
Vinay Kumar
Psychiatrist and Hindi poet from Patna. He has also written prose on psychology.

h: The ideal partner: a show that breaks down in everyday life
dek: The first instalment of Pallavi Vinod's new series on Sammukh says the picture of an ideal marriage is often something seen from the outside.
body: Sammukh has begun a weekly series on marriage, family and companionship, and the first instalment is an essay by fiction writer Pallavi Vinod. The editorial note recalls Erich Fromm's idea that the root of fascism lies in the patriarchal family, which itself rests on the institution of marriage. The series aims to open up the power, compromises and constraints inside marriage.

The essay begins with a friend whose relationship is breaking for the third time and who tells the writer, you will not understand my search, you have found the ideal partner. From here the question arises: what is an ideal partner anyway? Most people want a partner who cares about their happiness and dignity and stands by them in hard times. The demand is small, yet relationships that begin with passion often wear thin.

According to the writer, couples celebrating years together look ideal from outside, but up close the cracks show. She reads the rising cases of divorce and domestic violence this way: these problems existed before too, only the teaching to save the marriage at all costs kept them silent.

As an example she takes the film 'Marriage Story', in which Nicole, despite a devoted husband, feels she is losing her identity in the roles of mother and wife. Then her own story: she once saw the arguments in her home as a sign of an ideal family, and later understood that a healthy relationship also has room for disagreement and the freedom to turn down each other's views.
Finally she goes to the root of the word 'adarsh' (ideal), 'darsh', meaning to be seen, and says the ideal is perhaps less a lived truth and more a form put on show.
nazar: There is little honest conversation about marriage in Hindi; it is either romance or sermon. Sammukh's series looks at it as a question of power and equality, and that is what is needed, because women pay the biggest price for the silence inside the home. The idea that disagreement is a sign of a relationship's health applies even more to a politics that treats every question as rebellion than it does to families.
sawal: Is a relationship without disagreement truly one of equals?
ref: Erich Fromm
German-American psychoanalyst and social philosopher (1900-1980). In 'Escape from Freedom' he traced the roots of authoritarianism to the family and the mind.
Marriage Story
Noah Baumbach's 2019 American film. The story of a couple's divorce and the struggle within it.

h: Hari Bhatnagar's story 'Purza': when the hammer pounds the wall all night
dek: In this story published on Sammukh, an old teacher and his family are left alone against an influential builder, and the system quietly sides with the powerful.
body: Senior fiction writer Hari Bhatnagar's story 'Purza' (A Slip of Paper) has appeared on Sammukh as its Sunday story. According to the site's introduction, he has been associated with the Sahitya Akademi, has edited magazines such as 'Sakshatkar' and 'Kalavarta', and now brings out 'Rachna Samay'. The editorial note presents the story as showing how the system stands with the powerful and leaves the weak to their fate.

At the centre of the story is Kahkashan Masih, a retired geography teacher, who lives with his wife Farzana and daughter Sara in an old two-storey house next to a park full of garbage. Sara works at an organisation for children with disabilities and wants to fix up the damp ground floor for her work. The story is told by an old friend who has known this family for thirty years.

Next door, the son of a wealthy jeweller is a builder and former councillor who has faced corruption charges but keeps his clout. The old houses of the neighbourhood fell one by one, their people quietly disappeared, and luxurious bungalows came up. Then one day the surveyors arrive, and after that hammers start pounding the shared wall night after night.

The family complains to everyone from the police helpline to the police station to senior officers; nothing changes. A doctor laughs it off. Slowly, fear, loneliness and helplessness break Kahkashan in both body and mind, and the story moves through the hospital to an end where even the plea for justice remains unfinished.
The meaning of the story's title opens up at the end. In its weave it is as quiet as the eviction it records.
nazar: In this age of bulldozers and 'redevelopment', 'Purza' feels truer than any newspaper report. An old teacher and his small family, an influential builder, and a deaf system at every door: the story raises no slogan, it simply shows how cities swallow their old residents and no witness is left.
sawal: When no one hears his complaint, who will read his slip of paper?
ref: Hari Bhatnagar
Hindi fiction writer born in 1955 in Rath, Uttar Pradesh. His story 'Mai' is included in an NCERT textbook.
Purza
A small piece of paper on which a plea or message is written. In the story the word ties in with the final scene.

h: Sheru: our first anti-hero, who fled the village arena
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Shankhdhar Dubey's satire uses the family's first and last dog to laugh at bravery, pride and show.
body: This memoir-like satire from Shankhdhar Dubey's 'Shankhnaad' series is about a real dog, Sheru, who as far as the writer knows was his family's first and last pet. He calls him the family's first anti-hero, that is, a hero who fits no picture of a hero.

The story is set in the village. The writer's elder brother, fourteen or fifteen at the time, fell for the newborn puppy's white coat and innocent eyes and brought him home despite grandmother's objections. With a light jibe the writer notes that there were fights over male puppies but no takers for the females, and also that struggle made the females cleverer. The whole village knew about the birth in the straw shed.

Sheru was brought home like a trophy: a ring of bricks, a Dunlop bed and such protection that the children of the house grew jealous. But grown big and fat, Sheru turned out to be utterly timid. The elder brother had thought of him as an asset; he proved a burden.

Every week there were dog fights in the village, in which people sent in their gladiators. In the very first fight Sheru fled the ground, the brother lost face and stopped going there altogether. Sheru did not bark, walked with his tail between his legs, and later began snatching rotis from children and old people.

He lived a long life and died, and his cowardice left such a mark that no dog was ever kept in the house again. In the end the writer admits that when it comes to timidity, he himself is no less than Sheru.
nazar: This light satire is really a jab at the pressure of manliness and of becoming a 'lion' that shows up everywhere, from the village to the nation. Sheru was expected to raise the family's standing, and when he did not fight, the shame was the family's. In one line about the female puppies, the writer also quietly points at how daughters are treated.
sawal: Why is running from a fight always called cowardice?
ref: Anti-hero
A central character in a story who lacks traditional heroic qualities like bravery or morality. Yet the story revolves around him.
Shankhnaad
Shankhdhar Dubey's series of satirical pieces on Hindwi's Bela, poking fun at society through memories of village and home.
